title: Containing Agent Chaos — Solomon Hykes, Dagger

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 49%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk introduces 'container use,' an open-source developer tool providing containerized execution environments for coding agents, fitting the substrate-other-engineers-use criterion. The tool is built on Dagger for software builders (developer_platforms) and specifically targets coding assistants like Claude Code, Goose, and Codex (coding_assistants). The talk covers development (agents building software in containers), testing (git-based collaboration loop), and deployment (shipping containerized agent environments). The talk requires familiarity with containers, coding agents, MCP, and git workflows but remains accessible to AI engineering practitioners. A conference talk at the AI Engineer World's Fair featuring live demonstrations of the container use tool with coding agents. Nine direct transcript evidence anchors support the classification across the tool's purpose, architecture, and demonstrations.

summary: Solomon Hykes, creator of Docker and founder/CEO of Dagger, opens by noting he is speaking on the same stage he used for Docker Con 2015 almost exactly ten years prior. He frames the challenge of coding agent chaos from a platform engineering perspective, noting platform engineers enable others to ship software and that this role is evolving to include enabling agents. He identifies two current approaches to scaling agents: 'yolo mode' (running multiple agents sharing one environment, causing collisions) and all-in-one cloud services (which handle everything but limit control and create lock-in). Neither is sufficient. He articulates four desired capabilities: background work without constant oversight, rails to constrain agents to known-good configurations and tools, an efficient middle-ground intervention mechanism, and optionality to mix and match models, compute, and infrastructure. These map to four environment properties: isolated, customizable, multiplayer, and open. He argues containers are foundational but underutilized for agent workflows because existing tools were built for humans. He introduces 'container use' — analogous to computer use and browser use — where agents develop inside containers natively, distinct from merely sandboxing agent output. He demonstrates this with Claude Code via MCP integration, showing ephemeral containers running per action, state persisted in git objects alongside the repo, and no pollution of the local workspace. The demo continues with a `cu` command-line tool for listing and managing environments, inspecting what the agent sees (files and tools like Go version), and a collaboration loop using git-based history where snapshots function as commits. He highlights secrets integration with existing password managers like 1Password, remote execution on his home server with seamless file streaming, and the ability to merge or discard environments at will. He shows parallel agent experiments by invoking multiple agents (Claude Yolo, Goose) on the same environment, throwing away failed experiments without cleanup. A watch command displays real-time state snapshotting and branch divergence. Services running inside containers are tunneled to his local machine on distinct ports without conflicts. Hykes emphasizes the system is powered by Dagger, is open source, and runs anywhere — local, remote servers, CI, or clusters. He closes by live open-sourcing the project on stage at github.com/dagger/container-use, echoing his Docker Con tradition, while candidly acknowledging the software is unfinished but built on strong foundations: git, Dagger, and existing agents.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Coding agents create operational chaos; current scaling approaches (yolo mode or all-in-one cloud services) are both insufficient
Four desired agent system capabilities: background work, rails/constraints, efficient human intervention, and optionality
Four required environment properties: isolated, customizable, multiplayer, and open
'Container use' means agents develop inside containers natively — distinct from merely sandboxing agent output after the fact
Container use uses ephemeral containers per action with git-based state snapshotting, enabling a collaboration loop between watching every action and waiting for PRs
Environments are disposable: failed experiments can be thrown away without manual cleanup, enabling parallel agent experimentation

sections.title: Opening & Docker Con 2015 Reference
sections.summary: Solomon Hykes opens by noting he is on the exact same stage he used to kick off Docker Con 2015 almost exactly ten years prior to the day.

sections.title: Chaos in Coding Agents & Platform Engineering Perspective
sections.summary: Hykes discusses the chaos emerging from coding agents from a platform engineering perspective, noting platform engineers enable others to ship software and that this role is evolving to include enabling agents.

sections.title: Current Scaling Approaches & Their Limitations
sections.summary: Describes two current options for scaling agents: 'yolo mode' (running multiple agents sharing one environment, causing collisions) and all-in-one cloud services (which handle everything but limit control and lock you into their stack). Both have significant limitations.

sections.title: Four Desired Capabilities for Agent Systems
sections.summary: Articulates four desired capabilities: background work without constant oversight, rails to constrain agents, efficient middle-ground intervention, and optionality to mix and match models, compute, and infrastructure.

sections.title: Required Environment Properties & Container Use Concept
sections.summary: Maps the four needs to four environment properties: isolated, customizable, multiplayer, and open. Argues containers are foundational but underutilized because existing tools were built for humans. Introduces 'container use' — agents developing inside containers natively.

sections.title: Live Demo: Container Use with Claude Code
sections.summary: Demonstrates container use with Claude Code building a Go web app via MCP. Shows ephemeral containers per action with snapshotting, state persisted in git objects alongside the repo, no pollution of local workspace. Emphasizes agent-agnostic and environment-agnostic design.

sections.title: Demo Continuation: Environment Inspection & Infrastructure
sections.summary: Shows the `cu` command-line tool for listing environments and opening terminals to inspect what the agent sees — files and tools like Go version. Mentions secrets integration with 1Password (not demoed per team advice). Reveals the demo runs on his home server about one mile away, streaming files seamlessly.

sections.title: Collaboration Loop & Parallel Agent Experiments
sections.summary: Demonstrates the git-based history as a collaboration loop — a happy medium between watching every action and waiting for PRs. Shows merging environments, then invoking multiple agents (Claude Yolo, Goose) in parallel for design experiments. Emphasizes discarding failed environments without cleanup.

sections.title: Watch Command, Service Tunneling & Infrastructure Flexibility
sections.summary: Shows the watch command displaying real-time state snapshotting and branch divergence as agents work, built on thinly-wrapped git commands. Demonstrates services running inside containerized agent environments tunneled to his local machine on distinct ports without conflicts. Notes infrastructure flexibility: local, remote, CI, or clusters.

sections.title: Live Open-Sourcing on Stage
sections.summary: Closes by live open-sourcing the project on stage at github.com/dagger/container-use, echoing the Docker Con tradition of open-sourcing on stage. Candidly acknowledges the software is unfinished but built on strong foundations: git, Dagger, and existing agents. Invites community participation.

demonstrations: Live demo of 'container use' with Claude Code building a Go web app homepage via MCP, showing ephemeral containers per action and git-based state persistence
Demo of `cu` command-line tool for listing environments, opening terminals to inspect agent-visible files and tools, viewing git-based history of snapshots
Demo of collaboration loop: merging environments, invoking multiple agents (Claude Yolo, Goose) in parallel for design experiments, discarding failed environments without cleanup
Demo of watch command showing real-time state snapshotting and branch divergence as agents work
Demo of service tunneling: agent-run services in containers tunneled to local machine on distinct ports without conflicts
Live open-sourcing of the project on stage at github.com/dagger/container-use
limitations: The demoed software is unfinished and the speaker repeatedly acknowledges this, including during the live open-sourcing
Speaker admits being terrible at using Claude Code and needing aliases for permission flags
Secrets integration (e.g., 1Password) was not demoed because the team warned it would break
The live demo had messy moments with agents not completing tasks and some visible disorganization
All-in-one cloud agent services described as limiting control and creating lock-in
Yolo mode described as agents stepping on each other's toes when sharing an environment
quantitativeClaims: Home server running demo was approximately one mile from the conference venue
